title: PA House Republicans Launch ‘Freedom Through Affordability’ Initiative to Cut Costs for Families
raw_text:
PA House Republicans Launch ‘Freedom Through Affordability’ Initiative to Cut Costs for Families
March 25, 2026
HARRISBURG
—With Pennsylvanians facing rising costs on everyday essentials, House Republican policymakers today launched their “Freedom Through Affordability” initiative – a plan to deliver tax relief and lower costs to make Pennsylvania a more affordable place to live, work, and raise a family.
The initiative, unveiled at a Capitol press conference, includes a package of six-month tax cuts and sales tax holidays, a multi-billion-dollar relief effort, aimed at providing immediate relief to families and workers struggling under the weight of higher prices.
Framing the effort, Rep. David Rowe (R-Snyder/Union/Mifflin/Juniata), chairman of the House Republican Policy Committee, emphasized the direct connection between affordability and opportunity.
“Our goal is simple: Make Pennsylvania a place where families can afford to live, work and build their future. When people can keep more of what they earn and the cost of everyday life is within reach, they have the freedom to make their own choices about their future. That’s what this effort is about – achieving freedom through affordability for people across the Commonwealth,” said Rowe.
At the center of the initiative are targeted proposals designed to provide immediate relief on some of the most pressing household expenses, including the suspension of key taxes for six months, directly reducing costs on essential services and daily expenses.
Rowe is sponsoring legislation to reduce the state Personal Income Tax rate from 3.07% to 2.99% for six months.
Reps. Kristin Marcell (R-Bucks), vice chair of the House Republican Policy Committee, and Eric Davanzo (R-Westmoreland) are co-sponsoring legislation to suspend the Gross Receipts Tax on electricity and telecommunications for six months.
Highlighting the impact on everyday families, Marcell pointed to the growing pressure households are facing.
"Everywhere I go in my community, people are looking for a break from rising costs, especially on the basics of life,” said Marcell. “This temporary tax holiday is a commonsense way to give them that break, save them some money and help make life just a little easier."
Davanzo underscored how energy costs ripple throughout the broader economy.
“The message from Pennsylvanians has never been louder or more clear: Energy costs are making their day-to-day unaffordable. Right here and now, we can give families a little bit of breathing room and help them stretch their budgets a little bit further,” Davanzo said. “Because energy costs factor into production, wholesale and retail costs on everyday products, this relief will be felt across the Commonwealth’s entire economy.”
Focusing on transportation, Rep. Abby Major (R-Armstrong/Westmoreland) emphasized the burden of fuel costs on working families in introducing legislation to suspend the state’s gas tax for six months.
“High fuel costs compound the financial strain Pennsylvanians already face due to inflation and ongoing cost-of-living increases,” Major said. “My legislation will provide temporary relief to make it easier to balance a family’s budget. I urge immediate action so there is more money in the pockets of our hardworking residents.”
Affordability Starts Here Tour
In addition to advancing immediate relief, lawmakers stressed the importance of continuing to hear directly from residents across the Commonwealth.
Rep. Joe Hogan (R-Bucks), deputy chair of the Policy Committee, announced the launch of the “Affordability Starts Here” tour, which will bring lawmakers across the Commonwealth to hear directly from families, workers and employers about what it takes to make life more affordable.
“As the Policy Committee’s Deputy Chair on affordability, I know how important this ‘Affordability Starts Here’ Tour of Pennsylvania is for so many families,” said Hogan. “Starting next week, we will make our first stop in Hanover for a hearing on how we can reduce the costs of child care and expand the tour to all sectors of our economy. Folks across our Commonwealth have great ideas and I’m looking forward to identifying and promoting more ways to make Pennsylvania more affordable for everyone.”
Hogan, a new father, joins Rep. KC Tomlinson (R-Bucks) in co-sponsoring six-month sales tax holidays on car seats as well as newborn/baby products.
Additional members sponsoring affordability-related tax relief proposals include Reps. Mike Armanini (R-Clearfield/Elk), Stephanie Borowicz (R-Clinton/Union), Marla Brown (R- Lawrence), Jamie Flick (R-Lycoming/Union), Ann Flood (R-Northampton), Jonathan Fritz (R-Wayne/Susquehanna), Josh Kail (R-Beaver/Washington), Kate Klunk (R-York), Roman Kozak (R-Beaver), Thomas Kutz (R-Cumberland), Andrew Kuzma (R-Allegheny/Washington), Shelby Labs (R-Bucks), Robert Leadbeter (R-Columbia), Zach Mako (R-Lehigh/Northampton), Natalie Mihalek (R-Allegheny/Washington), Brett Miller (R-Lancaster), Brenda Pugh (R-Luzerne), Brian Rasel (R-Westmoreland), Chad Reichard (R-Franklin), Michael Stender (R-Northumberland/Montour) and Parke Wentling (R-Mercer). Legislation is forthcoming.

December 18, 2025
HARRISBURG
– Rep. Natalie Mihalek (R-Allegheny/Washington) today announced more than $1 million in Local Share Account grants were awarded to several local governments within the 40th Legislative District, supporting infrastructure projects and community development projects.
The grants, under the Local Share Account program, support economic development, job training, community improvement and public interest projects through gaming funds collected under the Pennsylvania Race Horse Development and Gaming Act (Act 71 of 2004).
“Our local officials work hard to keep taxes reasonable, while also delivering on the community projects our families deserve,” said Mihalek. “I can think of no better use of these dollars than to see these projects advance.”
Mihalek acknowledged the work of her colleagues in the General Assembly, such as Sen. Devlin Robinson (R-Allegheny), who called the grants a reflection of “our commitment to strengthening communities, improving public safety, and supporting local governments and nonprofits in their efforts to serve residents.”
Grants awarded to the 40th Legislative District include:
•
Municipality of Bethel Park - $662,198 to repair or replace sewer pipe at 100 Acres Drive, reducing infiltration at the Piney Fork Treatment Plant.
•
Municipality of Bethel Park - $59,637 to upgrade the audiovisual capabilities of meeting and event spaces at the Bethel Park Community Center.
•
Upper St. Clair Township - $165,604 to enhance the recently renovated Upper St. Clair Library by installing new, ADA-compliant shelving that improves accessibility and organization.
•

title: Upper St. Clair, Bethel Park Projects Awarded Grants, Mihalek Says
raw_text:
Upper St. Clair, Bethel Park Projects Awarded Grants, Mihalek Says
November 18, 2025
HARRISBURG – Rep. Natalie Mihalek (R-Allegheny/Washington) announced the Pennsylvania Commonwealth Financing Authority has approved grant awards in the Municipality of Bethel Park and Upper St. Clair Township. The more than $600,000 in grants come from the Allegheny Gaming Economic Development Tourism Fund (GEDTF).
"Projects like these are tangible and worthwhile investments that improve neighborhoods, and exactly the investments that Harrisburg can and should be delivering on," Mihalek said. “Both projects involve significant community hubs that also lure visitors who then patronize our local businesses, so it makes sense that grant dollars are invested this way.”
In Upper St. Clair, Gilfillan Farm was awarded just over $450,000 for several renovations; including the removal of two cisterns, masonry work, utility upgrades and excavation projects. Mihalek: House Leader Should Not Put Political Wins Over Water Safety
July 1, 2026
HARRISBURG – In a letter Rep. Natalie Mihalek (R-Allegheny/Washington) sent to House Majority Leader Rep. Matt Bradford (D-Montgomery) yesterday regarding improving safety on Pennsylvania waterways, she recommended if the majority leader is committed to making the topic a political one, her bill be reintroduced by a member of his own caucus.
“I get the political aspects of this business, but let’s face it – this is far from a political issue,” Mihalek said. “Nevertheless, if the win-loss column is of greater concern to Leader Bradford than doing the right thing by Pennsylvania’s hundreds of thousands of recreational boaters and swimmers, so be it. Let’s just get it done.”
The 2022 loss of Bethel Park teacher Jon Gentile motivated Mihalek to introduce legislation. Gentile fell victim to a low head dam while kayaking. Low head dams are highly dangerous because of the recirculating current they cause and because they are often invisible to approaching boaters and swimmers. Mihalek found that Pennsylvania leads the nation in deaths related to what have been dubbed “drowning machines.”
House Bill 961
was introduced in March 2025 and passed unanimously by the House Game and Fisheries Committee in November 2025. The proposal, which would require dams to be prominently marked with signs, has not been scheduled for a floor vote by House Democrats who control the chamber agenda because of their slim majority in the House.
In the letter, Mihalek told the majority leader that although some topics are rooted in partisan politics, this one is not.
“Rather than risk another loss of life, I ask you to please call the bill up for an immediate vote or take the proposal within House Bill 961 and introduce it in your name or that of a member on your side of the aisle,” the letter states. “Whichever path you choose, let’s get this done. I do not need credit for my work. I need to know that I have done everything in my power to get this across the finish line.”

Gaydos, Mihalek, Shaffer and Policy Committee Highlight Need for Accountability in Second-Degree Murder Sentencing
August 14, 2026
ALLEGHENY COUNTY
—Pennsylvania’s lack of a clear sentencing framework for second-degree murder could produce inconsistent sentences, overwhelm courts and force victims’ families to repeatedly relive the murders of their loved ones, prosecutors testified Thursday during a House Republican Policy Committee hearing.
The hearing, “Protecting Pennsylvania: Accountability and Justice in Second-Degree Murder Sentencing,” was hosted by Reps. Valerie Gaydos (R-Moon Township), Natalie Mihalek (R-Allegheny) and Jeremy Shaffer (R-Allegheny) at the Moon Township Municipal Building.
In March, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled that automatically imposing life without parole in every second-degree murder case, without considering an offender’s individual role and level of responsibility, violates the Pennsylvania Constitution. The court gave the General Assembly 120 days to establish a new sentencing framework, but the deadline passed without a final measure reaching the governor’s desk.
“No court ruling or legislative action can undo the loss these families have endured, but we can ensure their voices are heard and respected as Pennsylvania determines its path forward,” said House Republican Policy Committee Chairman David H. Rowe (R-Snyder/Union/Mifflin/Juniata). “Victims’ families deserve more than uncertainty. They deserve meaningful participation in the process and confidence that the justice system will never forget the life that was taken.”
Rowe opened the hearing by reading letters submitted by Stella Getgen and Christine Hickman, the wife and sister of murder victim Todd Getgen. Both described the loss their family has endured since his 2010 murder and the renewed trauma caused by the possibility that his killer’s sentence could be reconsidered.
Todd Getgen’s son was 6 years old when his father was murdered and has grown up without him. In her letter, Stella Getgen described having to explain to her young son why his father would never return, while assuring him that the man responsible would remain in prison. Hickman wrote that while her brother’s killer received life, Todd “didn’t get life; he got death.”
“Pennsylvania must get second-degree murder sentencing right—for victims, families and public safety,” said Gaydos. “Law enforcement has made clear how serious this issue is, yet without a consistent sentencing framework, our judicial system is in chaos and public safety is in jeopardy. Pennsylvanians should be outraged that House Philadelphia Democrats chose politics over public safety. It’s time to restore the rule of law, hold violent offenders accountable and demand that House Democrats take up this legislation immediately.”
Testimony was provided by Ronald M. Wabby Jr., deputy district attorney for the Critical Case Review Unit, Appellate Division, Allegheny County District Attorney’s Office; Westmoreland County District Attorney Nicole Ziccarelli; and Indiana County District Attorney Robert Manzi.
Wabby said Allegheny County has more than 160 individuals convicted of second-degree murder in cases dating to the 1970s. Drawing on his experience with juvenile-lifer resentencings, he warned that without a statewide framework, inconsistent sentences and years of additional appeals could force victims’ families to repeatedly revisit murders committed decades earlier.
“There is no finality that I can give a victim,” Wabby testified. “When a victim is forced to relive events decades later, I can’t explain to you the pain I saw in these people’s eyes.”
Mihalek, a former Allegheny County prosecutor, criticized House leaders for allowing partisan politics to derail a bipartisan sentencing solution, stressing that accountability for violent offenders is fundamental to public safety.
"In a day and age when the average Pennsylvania resident is done with partisan nonsense, House leaders played a dangerous game by waiting until the final hours of the court's deadline to amend a commonsense bill first passed by the Senate," Mihalek said. "Holding accountable violent criminals, convicted of some of the most atrocious crimes possible against their fellow man, is not a political game – it's a cornerstone of public safety. I'm happy to discuss prison reforms for nonviolent offenders and offering hands up to help them change their lives, but I am completely opposed to simply unlocking the cell doors for Pennsylvania's most violent criminals."
Ziccarelli testified that approximately 1,100 people currently serving second-degree murder sentences could seek resentencing or possible release. She said the resulting proceedings would impose significant costs on taxpayers, strain courts and prosecutors, and jeopardize public safety.
She recommended preserving victims’ statutory rights to participate in parole proceedings, protecting the finality of plea agreements and establishing a mandatory minimum sentence while retaining life without parole for the most serious cases.
Ziccarelli also discussed a pending Westmoreland County case involving the murder of Anthony Williams, a 31-year-old father of five. His family waited five years for a jury verdict but continues to await a final sentence because no legislative framework is in place.
Manzi rejected portrayals of second-degree murder defendants as innocent bystanders. He explained that a conviction requires participation as a principal or accomplice in an underlying felony such as robbery, rape, arson, burglary or kidnapping, during which a death occurs. He then detailed several Indiana County cases involving shootings, beatings and other brutal murders.
Shaffer said testimony from law enforcement underscored the seriousness of the issue and the need for a statewide solution that protects victims’ families and ensures uniform justice.
“I’ve expressed my disappointment regarding the situation surrounding second-degree murder sentencing. It was good to hear from law enforcement officials about the seriousness of this issue. We need to move forward with a solution to protect victims’ families and have uniform justice across the state,” said Shaffer.
The prosecutors expressed support for key elements of
Senate Bill 1400
, which would establish a minimum sentence of 35 years with a maximum of life imprisonment, preserve life without parole under specified circumstances, and create a structured parole process for certain people already serving second-degree murder sentences.
House Democrats amended
House Bill 1042
to remove the Senate’s bipartisan sentencing framework and add unrelated medical parole and other provisions. Those changes prevented the legislation from receiving final approval before the court’s deadline and perpetuated the legal uncertainty facing prosecutors, courts and victims’ families.
Written testimony was also submitted by John Rago, a Duquesne University Kline School of Law professor, Pennsylvania Commission on Sentencing member, and chairman of the Center for Victims board; the Pennsylvania State Troopers Association; and Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 91.
The House Republican Policy Committee will continue examining second-degree murder sentencing at another public hearing in the coming weeks.

Mihalek Announces More Than $1.75 Million in Local Share Account Grants for 40th District Projects
September 15, 2026
HARRISBURG – Rep. Natalie Mihalek (R-Allegheny/Washington), Sen. Camera Bartolotta (R-46) and Sen. Devlin Robinson (R-37) today announced more than $1.75 million in Local Share Account grants were awarded to local governments and authorities in the 40th Legislative District to support infrastructure, recreation and emergency services.
“Investing in our communities means making sure local projects have the support they need to move forward,” said Mihalek. “I’m pleased to see this funding provide support for projects that will improve the quality of life for residents and help our communities continue to grow.”
“I'm proud to have worked closely with Rep. Mihalek to secure this funding for Peters Township and the surrounding community,” said Bartolotta. “The Church Hill Road sewer line extension will bring aging properties up to modern health and safety standards while eliminating an outdated lift station. At Peterswood Park, a new turf soccer field will give families a high-quality space to enjoy for years to come. These are the kinds of projects that make a real difference in people's everyday lives.”
“I’m proud to work with Rep. Mihalek to secure this funding to better our communities,” said Robinson. “By working together, we were able to support Bethel Park in their modernization of local park electrical equipment and ensure Tri-Community South EMS has the resources they need to provide residents with life-saving services.”
Grants awarded to the 40th Legislative District include:
•
Municipality of Bethel Park – $52,195
to upgrade lighting control systems at Simmons Park, Millennium Park and Park Avenue fields. The project will allow municipal staff to remotely control field lighting and include new equipment, cabinets, conduits and wiring.
•
Peters Creek Sanitary Authority – $450,000
to extend sanitary sewer service along Church Hill Road in Peters Township. The project will install approximately 8,100 feet of force main, provide sewer service to 43 existing properties currently using private on-lot disposal systems and eliminate the Old Trail Lift Station, which currently serves approximately 200 customers.
•
Peters Township – $1 million
to restore the soccer fields at Peterswood Park. The project will replace the existing 133,200-square-foot soccer field with a high-performance turf system featuring permanent lines for soccer, football and lacrosse.
•
Upper St. Clair Township – $253,043
for the purchase of an emergency medical response vehicle for Tri-Community South EMS, which serves South Park Township, Upper St. Clair Township and the Municipality of Bethel Park. The funding will support the purchase of the vehicle and related equipment.
The grants, awarded through the Local Share Account program, support economic development, job training, community improvement and public interest projects through gaming funds collected under the Pennsylvania Race Horse Development and Gaming Act (Act 71 of 2004).

title: Gaydos, Mihalek, Shaffer and Policy Committee Highlight Need for Accountability in Second-Degree Murder Sentencing
raw_text:
Gaydos, Mihalek, Shaffer and Policy Committee Highlight Need for Accountability in Second-Degree Murder Sentencing
August 14, 2026
ALLEGHENY COUNTY
—Pennsylvania’s lack of a clear sentencing framework for second-degree murder could produce inconsistent sentences, overwhelm courts and force victims’ families to repeatedly relive the murders of their loved ones, prosecutors testified Thursday during a House Republican Policy Committee hearing.
The hearing, “Protecting Pennsylvania: Accountability and Justice in Second-Degree Murder Sentencing,” was hosted by Reps. Valerie Gaydos (R-Moon Township), Natalie Mihalek (R-Allegheny) and Jeremy Shaffer (R-Allegheny) at the Moon Township Municipal Building.
In March, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled that automatically imposing life without parole in every second-degree murder case, without considering an offender’s individual role and level of responsibility, violates the Pennsylvania Constitution. The court gave the General Assembly 120 days to establish a new sentencing framework, but the deadline passed without a final measure reaching the governor’s desk.
“No court ruling or legislative action can undo the loss these families have endured, but we can ensure their voices are heard and respected as Pennsylvania determines its path forward,” said House Republican Policy Committee Chairman David H. Rowe (R-Snyder/Union/Mifflin/Juniata). “Victims’ families deserve more than uncertainty. They deserve meaningful participation in the process and confidence that the justice system will never forget the life that was taken.”
Rowe opened the hearing by reading letters submitted by Stella Getgen and Christine Hickman, the wife and sister of murder victim Todd Getgen. Both described the loss their family has endured since his 2010 murder and the renewed trauma caused by the possibility that his killer’s sentence could be reconsidered.
Todd Getgen’s son was 6 years old when his father was murdered and has grown up without him. In her letter, Stella Getgen described having to explain to her young son why his father would never return, while assuring him that the man responsible would remain in prison. Hickman wrote that while her brother’s killer received life, Todd “didn’t get life; he got death.”
“Pennsylvania must get second-degree murder sentencing right—for victims, families and public safety,” said Gaydos. “Law enforcement has made clear how serious this issue is, yet without a consistent sentencing framework, our judicial system is in chaos and public safety is in jeopardy. Pennsylvanians should be outraged that House Philadelphia Democrats chose politics over public safety. It’s time to restore the rule of law, hold violent offenders accountable and demand that House Democrats take up this legislation immediately.”
Testimony was provided by Ronald M. Wabby Jr., deputy district attorney for the Critical Case Review Unit, Appellate Division, Allegheny County District Attorney’s Office; Westmoreland County District Attorney Nicole Ziccarelli; and Indiana County District Attorney Robert Manzi.
Wabby said Allegheny County has more than 160 individuals convicted of second-degree murder in cases dating to the 1970s. Drawing on his experience with juvenile-lifer resentencings, he warned that without a statewide framework, inconsistent sentences and years of additional appeals could force victims’ families to repeatedly revisit murders committed decades earlier.
“There is no finality that I can give a victim,” Wabby testified. “When a victim is forced to relive events decades later, I can’t explain to you the pain I saw in these people’s eyes.”
Mihalek, a former Allegheny County prosecutor, criticized House leaders for allowing partisan politics to derail a bipartisan sentencing solution, stressing that accountability for violent offenders is fundamental to public safety.
"In a day and age when the average Pennsylvania resident is done with partisan nonsense, House leaders played a dangerous game by waiting until the final hours of the court's deadline to amend a commonsense bill first passed by the Senate," Mihalek said. "Holding accountable violent criminals, convicted of some of the most atrocious crimes possible against their fellow man, is not a political game – it's a cornerstone of public safety. I'm happy to discuss prison reforms for nonviolent offenders and offering hands up to help them change their lives, but I am completely opposed to simply unlocking the cell doors for Pennsylvania's most violent criminals."
Ziccarelli testified that approximately 1,100 people currently serving second-degree murder sentences could seek resentencing or possible release. She said the resulting proceedings would impose significant costs on taxpayers, strain courts and prosecutors, and jeopardize public safety.
She recommended preserving victims’ statutory rights to participate in parole proceedings, protecting the finality of plea agreements and establishing a mandatory minimum sentence while retaining life without parole for the most serious cases.
Ziccarelli also discussed a pending Westmoreland County case involving the murder of Anthony Williams, a 31-year-old father of five. His family waited five years for a jury verdict but continues to await a final sentence because no legislative framework is in place.
Manzi rejected portrayals of second-degree murder defendants as innocent bystanders. He explained that a conviction requires participation as a principal or accomplice in an underlying felony such as robbery, rape, arson, burglary or kidnapping, during which a death occurs. He then detailed several Indiana County cases involving shootings, beatings and other brutal murders.
Shaffer said testimony from law enforcement underscored the seriousness of the issue and the need for a statewide solution that protects victims’ families and ensures uniform justice.
“I’ve expressed my disappointment regarding the situation surrounding second-degree murder sentencing. It was good to hear from law enforcement officials about the seriousness of this issue. We need to move forward with a solution to protect victims’ families and have uniform justice across the state,” said Shaffer.
The prosecutors expressed support for key elements of
Senate Bill 1400
, which would establish a minimum sentence of 35 years with a maximum of life imprisonment, preserve life without parole under specified circumstances, and create a structured parole process for certain people already serving second-degree murder sentences.
House Democrats amended
House Bill 1042
to remove the Senate’s bipartisan sentencing framework and add unrelated medical parole and other provisions. Those changes prevented the legislation from receiving final approval before the court’s deadline and perpetuated the legal uncertainty facing prosecutors, courts and victims’ families.
Written testimony was also submitted by John Rago, a Duquesne University Kline School of Law professor, Pennsylvania Commission on Sentencing member, and chairman of the Center for Victims board; the Pennsylvania State Troopers Association; and Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 91.
The House Republican Policy Committee will continue examining second-degree murder sentencing at another public hearing in the coming weeks.

Mihalek: House Leader Should Not Put Political Wins Over Water Safety
July 1, 2026
HARRISBURG – In a letter Rep. Natalie Mihalek (R-Allegheny/Washington) sent to House Majority Leader Rep. Matt Bradford (D-Montgomery) yesterday regarding improving safety on Pennsylvania waterways, she recommended if the majority leader is committed to making the topic a political one, her bill be reintroduced by a member of his own caucus.
“I get the political aspects of this business, but let’s face it – this is far from a political issue,” Mihalek said. “Nevertheless, if the win-loss column is of greater concern to Leader Bradford than doing the right thing by Pennsylvania’s hundreds of thousands of recreational boaters and swimmers, so be it. Let’s just get it done.”
The 2022 loss of Bethel Park teacher Jon Gentile motivated Mihalek to introduce legislation. Gentile fell victim to a low head dam while kayaking. Low head dams are highly dangerous because of the recirculating current they cause and because they are often invisible to approaching boaters and swimmers. Mihalek found that Pennsylvania leads the nation in deaths related to what have been dubbed “drowning machines.”
House Bill 961
was introduced in March 2025 and passed unanimously by the House Game and Fisheries Committee in November 2025. The proposal, which would require dams to be prominently marked with signs, has not been scheduled for a floor vote by House Democrats who control the chamber agenda because of their slim majority in the House.
In the letter, Mihalek told the majority leader that although some topics are rooted in partisan politics, this one is not.
“Rather than risk another loss of life, I ask you to please call the bill up for an immediate vote or take the proposal within House Bill 961 and introduce it in your name or that of a member on your side of the aisle,” the letter states. “Whichever path you choose, let’s get this done. I do not need credit for my work. I need to know that I have done everything in my power to get this across the finish line.”

PA House Republicans Launch ‘Freedom Through Affordability’ Initiative to Cut Costs for Families
March 25, 2026
HARRISBURG
—With Pennsylvanians facing rising costs on everyday essentials, House Republican policymakers today launched their “Freedom Through Affordability” initiative – a plan to deliver tax relief and lower costs to make Pennsylvania a more affordable place to live, work, and raise a family.
The initiative, unveiled at a Capitol press conference, includes a package of six-month tax cuts and sales tax holidays, a multi-billion-dollar relief effort, aimed at providing immediate relief to families and workers struggling under the weight of higher prices.
Framing the effort, Rep. David Rowe (R-Snyder/Union/Mifflin/Juniata), chairman of the House Republican Policy Committee, emphasized the direct connection between affordability and opportunity.
“Our goal is simple: Make Pennsylvania a place where families can afford to live, work and build their future. When people can keep more of what they earn and the cost of everyday life is within reach, they have the freedom to make their own choices about their future. That’s what this effort is about – achieving freedom through affordability for people across the Commonwealth,” said Rowe.
At the center of the initiative are targeted proposals designed to provide immediate relief on some of the most pressing household expenses, including the suspension of key taxes for six months, directly reducing costs on essential services and daily expenses.
Rowe is sponsoring legislation to reduce the state Personal Income Tax rate from 3.07% to 2.99% for six months.
Reps. Kristin Marcell (R-Bucks), vice chair of the House Republican Policy Committee, and Eric Davanzo (R-Westmoreland) are co-sponsoring legislation to suspend the Gross Receipts Tax on electricity and telecommunications for six months.
Highlighting the impact on everyday families, Marcell pointed to the growing pressure households are facing.
"Everywhere I go in my community, people are looking for a break from rising costs, especially on the basics of life,” said Marcell. “This temporary tax holiday is a commonsense way to give them that break, save them some money and help make life just a little easier."
Davanzo underscored how energy costs ripple throughout the broader economy.
“The message from Pennsylvanians has never been louder or more clear: Energy costs are making their day-to-day unaffordable. Right here and now, we can give families a little bit of breathing room and help them stretch their budgets a little bit further,” Davanzo said. “Because energy costs factor into production, wholesale and retail costs on everyday products, this relief will be felt across the Commonwealth’s entire economy.”
Focusing on transportation, Rep. Abby Major (R-Armstrong/Westmoreland) emphasized the burden of fuel costs on working families in introducing legislation to suspend the state’s gas tax for six months.
“High fuel costs compound the financial strain Pennsylvanians already face due to inflation and ongoing cost-of-living increases,” Major said. “My legislation will provide temporary relief to make it easier to balance a family’s budget. I urge immediate action so there is more money in the pockets of our hardworking residents.”
Affordability Starts Here Tour
In addition to advancing immediate relief, lawmakers stressed the importance of continuing to hear directly from residents across the Commonwealth.
Rep. Joe Hogan (R-Bucks), deputy chair of the Policy Committee, announced the launch of the “Affordability Starts Here” tour, which will bring lawmakers across the Commonwealth to hear directly from families, workers and employers about what it takes to make life more affordable.
“As the Policy Committee’s Deputy Chair on affordability, I know how important this ‘Affordability Starts Here’ Tour of Pennsylvania is for so many families,” said Hogan. “Starting next week, we will make our first stop in Hanover for a hearing on how we can reduce the costs of child care and expand the tour to all sectors of our economy. Folks across our Commonwealth have great ideas and I’m looking forward to identifying and promoting more ways to make Pennsylvania more affordable for everyone.”
Hogan, a new father, joins Rep. KC Tomlinson (R-Bucks) in co-sponsoring six-month sales tax holidays on car seats as well as newborn/baby products.

Mihalek: It’s Time for Majority Party Leaders, Shapiro to Act on Budget
July 10, 2025
HARRISBURG
– Rep. Natalie Mihalek (R-Allegheny/Washington) issued the below statement, calling on House majority party leaders and Gov. Josh Shapiro to take action on Pennsylvania’s late budget:
“Because the state budget is late more often than it is on time, some folks in Harrisburg would say today is not July 10, it’s June 40. But a late budget is no laughing matter.
“As stewards of taxpayer dollars, it is our duty to craft an on-time budget that works for the people of Pennsylvania.
“The residents of the 40th district sent me to Harrisburg to be an advocate for our region and to make policies that serve our Commonwealth without overspending and putting future generations on the hook for irresponsible fiscal decisions. Those will always be my top priorities.
“Unfortunately, the priority of the majority party is to play political games. Negotiations have been stalled for weeks, yet session days continue to be added so the House can vote on bills that have zero chance in the Senate, yet a very high probability of turning into political fodder being texted out to residents who are beyond frustrated with these games.
“It is time for Gov. Shapiro and the House Democrats to act like adults and get a responsible budget passed for this Commonwealth instead of acting like children without any structure to their summer.”
Representative Natalie Mihalek
40th Legislative District
Pennsylvania House of Representatives

title: Lawmakers, Advocates Rally for Passage of Venkat/Mihalek Bill to Protect Restaurant Patrons with Food Allergies
raw_text:
Lawmakers, Advocates Rally for Passage of Venkat/Mihalek Bill to Protect Restaurant Patrons with Food Allergies
June 10, 2025
HARRISBURG –– Lawmakers and food allergy advocates joined forces today to push for passage of legislation that would make the state’s restaurants and other food retail establishments safer for more than 1.3 million Pennsylvanians living with food allergies, according to the bill’s prime sponsors, state Reps. Arvind Venkat (D-Allegheny) and Natalie Mihalek (R-Allegheny/Westmoreland).
Venkat said
H.B. 77
– which passed the House earlier this year with strong bipartisan support – would reduce life-threatening risks by targeting practices in higher-risk settings, including restaurants and other retail food facilities, where patrons are often unknowingly exposed to allergens.
“As an emergency physician, I have treated hundreds of patients with life-threatening allergic reactions, including many food-based reactions that could have been prevented,” Venkat said. “As a lawmaker, I know we can do more to reduce that risk.
“One important way is by mandating changes in higher-risk settings like restaurants and other food retail facilities, where cross-contamination during food preparation, failing to notify customers about the need to convey their food allergies, or a patron’s failure to alert staff of food allergies accounts for many incidents. Earlier this year, the House passed our bill that would require these businesses to increase food allergy awareness among employees and customers. It’s an important step that would save lives.”
Mihalek said, “If you or someone you love suffers from food allergies, a little knowledge on the part of those who prepare and serve our foods can be the difference between life and death. The unfortunate reality is that more people are diagnosed with food allergies every day and the simple proposals in House Bill 77 are reasonable ways to provide them with confidence that their food is safe.”
Advocates from Food Allergy Research & Education (FARE) also voiced their support for the bill.
“We are grateful to Reps. Venkat and Mihalek for their leadership spearheading this effort and to Kathy Briden and her family for their fierce advocacy on this issue,” said FARE CEO Sung Poblete, RN, PhD. “We believe House Bill 77 creates a mutually beneficial solution for the food allergy community and the state’s restaurants.
“With a practical law in place, individuals and families living with food allergy may be more willing to extend trust when dining out, allowing Pennsylvania restaurants to reap the economic benefits from engaging with our sizeable community. By passing this legislation, Pennsylvania will become a model state for food allergy awareness and a culinary destination for food allergy patients and families.”
The Pennsylvania Restaurant & Lodging Association supports the legislation, as well.
“As the association representing thousands of restaurants, bars, caterers and other hospitality businesses across Pennsylvania, PRLA recognizes the critical importance of food allergy awareness in protecting the health and safety of our guests,” said Joe Massaro, president and CEO of PRLA. “Many of our members already have strong food allergy protocols in place, while others are seeking guidance and best practices. We believe House Bill 77 supports this effort by establishing clear, reasonable standards that are not overly burdensome for operators across the commonwealth.”
Also speaking at the event was advocate Kathy Briden, whose son Matthew died after accidentally being exposed to peanuts while eating at a restaurant in Allegheny County.
House Bill 77 would require restaurants and food retail establishments to display informational posters advising employees about major food allergens and the symptoms of an allergic reaction. These businesses would also be required to include a statement on their menu or other written notice to customers about food allergens used, and a request that customers inform the employees serving them about any food allergies.
The bill passed the House in February by a strong bipartisan majority and is now in the Senate Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee.
It’s estimated that more than 1.3 million Pennsylvanians – including approximately 200,000 children – live with food allergies.

title: Healthy PA Legislative Package Gains Momentum After Testimony, Press Event, Says Mihalek
raw_text:
Healthy PA Legislative Package Gains Momentum After Testimony, Press Event, Says Mihalek
May 15, 2025
HARRISBURG
– The Consumer Protection Committee of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives held a hearing this week on the eight bills included in the Healthy PA legislative package. State Rep. Natalie Mihalek (R-Allegheny/Washington), author of the package, along with several other lawmakers held a press conference following the testimony.
“We must demand scrutiny beyond the assurances of industry that what we are eating is safe,” Mihalek said. “When the seller and scientist are one and the same, how can the average consumer differentiate between marketing and science.
“The time has come to clean up our food supply. For too long, we have been bombarded with chemicals, dyes andinferior artificial ingredients only to suffer serious health consequences from ingesting the foods that are readily available to us. Since the federal government has failed to protect us, we have a duty to act in the state legislature to protect the people of Pennsylvania. We cannot afford to wait.”
The Environmental Working Group, Rodale Institute, Michael J. Fox foundation, Kellyn Foundation and Unleaded Kids provided supporting testifiers who laid out the case for each of the bills in the package. Opposition testimony came from the International Association of Color Manufacturers, the National Confectioners Association and the PA Chamber, who are in favor of the status quo regarding food safety.
During the press event, Mihalek unveiled the “Trillion Dollar Tree.” Mihalek stated, “Think of our collective health like a tree, with chronic diseases for branches and at the root of that tree we have metabolic dysfunction. Toxic chemicals from our food are constantly attacking the root. We spend $5 trillion every year treating the branches and absolutely nothing fighting back against what is attacking our roots. It’s time to change that.
“I am so grateful to the 40 bipartisan co-sponsors for their advocacy on this issue,” continued Mihalek. “Together we will create a path forward for the Pennsylvania consumer.”
In addition to the hearing and press event, advocates were on hand in the Capitol educating other lawmakers on the importance of these bills.
